description: Universal SAS->pandas gotchas applied to every conversion: case sensitivity, SUM vs +, dates, dtypes, float tolerance, blanks, char truncation, missing semantics, column order, and merge overwrites.

g01_case_insensitive_columns.title: Column names are case-insensitive in SAS but case-sensitive in pandas -- preserve exact output names.
rule: SAS treats `Queue` and `queue` as the same variable; pandas does not.
Preserve the exact output column names the SAS step produces -- do not silently re-case.

g02_sum_ignores_missing.title: SAS SUM() ignores missing; Python + propagates NaN.
rule: SAS `sum(a, b, c)` skips missing values; Python `a + b + c` yields `NaN` if any operand is `NaN`.
Use a row-wise sum that skips NaN to match SAS SUM().

code: df["total"] = df[["a", "b", "c"]].sum(axis=1)   # matches SAS SUM(), skips NaN

g03_sas_dates.title: SAS dates: know whether you have an integer day-count (origin 1960) or a formatted string.
rule: A raw SAS integer is a day count with origin **1960-01-01** (not the 1970 Unix epoch); the wrong epoch shifts every date by 10 years.
A formatted string like `15JAN1980` (`date9.`) is text, NOT a day count -- do not use `origin=` on it (it raises); parse the format instead.
Check the dtype: an object/string column is the formatted-string case, a numeric column is the integer case.
`intck('year', start, end)` counts year **boundaries crossed** = `end.year - start.year` (not age at last birthday); `intck('month', ...)` = `(end.year-start.year)*12 + (end.month-start.month)`.
pitfalls: Using the default unix epoch (1970) on a raw SAS integer shifts dates 10 years.
Passing origin= together with a string date raises 'str is not compatible with origin'.

code: # (a) raw SAS integer day-count -- origin 1960-01-01, NOT unix 1970:
# (b) formatted date string like '15JAN1980' (date9.) -- parse, do not use origin=:
# intck('year', a, b) = boundaries crossed = b.year - a.year:

g04_validate_dtypes.title: Validate data types; cast id/date columns explicitly.
rule: A SAS numeric with missing values becomes a float in pandas, which breaks joins on id-like columns (`100010.0` vs `100010`).
Cast deliberately: nullable integer for ids, datetime for dates.
pitfalls: Joining on a float-demoted id column silently drops matches.

g05_float_tolerance.title: Compare numbers within tolerance; rounding conventions differ (banker's vs half-up).
rule: SAS and Python can differ in the last decimals, and Python `round()` uses banker's (half-even) rounding while SAS uses half-up.
Never compare floats with `==`; use a tolerance, and make rounding explicit when a convention is required.
pitfalls: Python's half-even round() disagrees with SAS half-up on .5 boundaries.

g06_trailing_blanks.title: SAS ignores trailing blanks; pandas does not -- strip character keys.
rule: SAS stores characters in fixed-width fields and ignores trailing spaces when comparing (`"CABCD"` == `"CABCD "`).
Strip character keys before join/filter.
pitfalls: Unstripped trailing spaces make otherwise-equal keys fail to join.

g07_char_truncation.title: SAS silently truncates characters to the declared length, set by the FIRST value assigned.
rule: A `$5` variable stores `CABCDE` as `CABCD`. Only replicate truncation when the SAS field genuinely truncated (to keep keys matching); otherwise keep the full value.
The length is set by the **FIRST literal assigned in program order**, not the longest. Later, longer literals are truncated to that width.
Scan the assignments in source order, take `len(first_literal)`, and slice every value of that variable to it. A later explicit `LENGTH var $n;` overrides this.
pitfalls: income_band whose first literal is 'HIGH' is $4, so 'MEDIUM'->'MEDI' and 'UNKNOWN'->'UNKN' -- a classic silent QC mismatch.

code: df["queue"] = df["queue"].str.slice(0, 5)   # only to match a genuinely truncated SAS $5 field
# length fixed by first literal in program order (here 'HIGH' -> $4):

g08_missing_semantics.title: Missing-value semantics are richer in SAS; groupby must keep the missing-key group.
rule: SAS has numeric missing (`.`), 28 special missings (`.A`-`.Z`, `._`), and empty strings (`''`); pandas collapses these to `NaN`/`None`.
SAS keeps missing key values as their own group, while pandas `groupby` drops NaN keys by default -- pass `dropna=False`.
pitfalls: Default groupby drops NaN-key rows, losing the missing-key group SAS keeps.

code: df.groupby("queue", dropna=False)["vol"].sum()   # keep the missing-key group

g09_column_order.title: Column order is part of output correctness.
rule: Even with all the right columns, a different order fails structural QC.
Set the expected column order explicitly on the final output.

g10_overlapping_merge_columns.title: Overlapping non-key columns in a merge: SAS overwrites left with right.
rule: When both inputs share non-key columns, SAS overwrites left with right; pandas adds `_x`/`_y` suffixes.
Decide explicitly which side wins and drop/rename so the output columns match SAS.
pitfalls: Leaving _x/_y suffixes in the output diverges from the single SAS column.
